Brisbane-based software firm Octopus Deploy took on a fresh $US30 million ($45.4 million) investment from US venture capital giant Insight Partners to fund its first major acquisition last year, with newly published accounts show the company has traded dividends and profits for significant revenue growth since its major 2021 investment.

The 13-year-old husband and wife run firm was unheard of outside techie circles until it shocked the local market [by locking in a $US172.5 million investment from the New York-based VC firm](https://www.afr.com/technology/brisbane-couple-builds-tech-giant-on-the-quiet-20210419-p57kix) in April 2021. It has now filed accounts covering 2020 to 2024 with the corporate regulator, which show it has adopted a less conservative fiscal approach since the investment.

![](https://static.ffx.io/images/$zoom_0.2%2C$multiply_3%2C$ratio_1.5%2C$width_756%2C$x_0%2C$y_22/t_crop_custom/c_scale%2Cw_620%2Cq_88%2Cf_auto/850a0f21349340700a947d17aba49508655f57ad)

Husband and wife Paul and Sonia Stovell founded Octopus Deploy in 2011.   Tertius Pickard

The documents show the company was profitable before Insight Partners bought in, paying out $US2.7 million in dividends in 2020. It has made losses since 2021, which narrowed in 2024, but its revenue has almost tripled in that time.

In an interview to discuss the financial reports, co-founder and chief executive Paul Stovell revealed the company has no plans to test the public markets or raise fresh capital in the near future, but that [its $US28 million buyout of US tech firm Codefresh](https://www.afr.com/link/follow-20180101-p5f7eu) last year had followed the new $US30 million investment.

The company makes tools to help software developers release code more quickly and with fewer errors. In its latest accounts it booked revenue of $US54.7 million last year, with a loss of $US1.6 million.

Advertisement

The 2021 investment had valued Octopus Deploy at $US500 million and, despite softening private tech company valuations since, the fresh capital injection increased this slightly to $US580 million, albeit on a less generous revenue multiple.

In its first full year with Insight Partners managing director Michael Triplett in the boardroom, the company went from an after-tax profit of $US2 million in 2021 to a loss of $US2.7 million in 2022 as it more than doubled spending on staff, and sales and marketing.

![](https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/aAydo/full.png)

Octopus Deploy’s losses widened the following year, peaking at $US8.4 million for the 12 months ended June 30, 2023. It has not paid dividends since 2020.

Over the same period, revenue has rocketed from $US19.6 million in the 2021 financial year to $US54.7 million in 2024.

“We’d been very profitable,” Stovell said. “I think we were possibly holding ourselves back by trying to run the company so profitably that we weren’t always experimenting or trying things that would set us up for this kind of growth.”

Advertisement

That mindset shifted when Insight joined the share register, Stovell said.

He said the company’s growth has come from selling more software subscriptions to bigger customers with large software engineering teams, such as banks and insurance companies.

More than 140 of the company’s 4000 customers spend more than $US100,000 on its products each year, up from just 17 when Insight invested in 2021.

Insight Partners now owns 37 per cent of the company’s stock while Stovell and his wife Sonia Stovell, who co-founded Octopus Deploy with him in 2012, retain 47 per cent.

Stovell said there was no pressure on him to go public, despite the company beginning to publish quarterly performance updates six months ago.

Advertisement

“At some point we expect our investor base will broaden, and we also think that public transparency is a good light to shine on things and helps make the company better,” he said. “We thought, why not start sharing it now and let people know how the business is going?”

The latest data showed Octopus Deploy’s annual recurring revenue hit $US80 million in August. Annualised revenue is a measure favoured by fast-growing technology firms which extrapolates the latest month’s revenue over a 12-month period.

[Like Canva and Atlassian,](https://www.afr.com/technology/rare-glimpse-into-canva-accounts-questions-its-profit-story-20250921-p5mwnv) Stovell said the company would focus on remaining profitable on a cash-flow basis, rather than on accounting measures like net profit after tax.

“In our view, a company should be able to stand on its own without needing investor funds to keep the operations going,” he said.
